wi_devil_s_lake_bouldering.blurb: The boulder-heavy side of Devil's Lake State Park sits in the Baraboo Range just south of the town of Baraboo, roughly 35 miles northwest of Madison. Steep quartzite bluffs tower about 500 feet over the lake, with big talus slopes below them and scattered blocks through the forest. Nearly all of the climbing here is bouldering, plus a modest number of trad lines and top ropes. Difficulty runs the full range: a wide base of V0 to V4, a deep middle band, and a thinner tail of hard problems into the double digits. East Bluff and West Bluff hold most of the problems, with South Bluff, Burma Road and Steinke Basin adding more variety. The quartzite is hard, smooth and glassy, so friction is scarce and grades can feel stiffer than the number suggests. Expect a forested, scenic setting that is easy to reach from Madison.

co_estes_park_valley.blurb: Climbing around the mountain town of Estes Park spreads over granite and gneiss cliffs at roughly 7,500 feet, along with boulders and crags tucked into the nearby canyons and the edge of Rocky Mountain National Park. Trad leads, with a large block of sport routes and a smaller number of boulder problems, top ropes and a little ice. Grades center on 5.9 to 5.11, with a decent supply of 5.7 and 5.8 and a hard tail up to 5.13 and beyond. Lumpy Ridge is the trad heartland, with walls, pillars and spires reached by walks of a few miles. Big Thompson Canyon mixes sport and trad on short approaches, and the Highway 7 canyons and Devil's Gulch add more. Summer and fall are the main season, and old-school grades can feel stout, so warm up below your limit.

nc_1_southern_mountains_region.blurb: This is the mountainous southwest corner of North Carolina, spread over the Blue Ridge around Brevard, Cashiers and the Chimney Rock area. Trad climbing leads, followed by a big bouldering scene, a small sport selection and a little ice in cold snaps. Most roped climbs fall between 5.8 and 5.12, with the greatest numbers around 5.10 and 5.11, while boulder problems run from easy to V10 and beyond. Looking Glass Rock and Cedar Rock give domed multi-pitch faces, Laurel Knob and Whiteside Mountain bring longer, bolder lines, and Rumbling Bald offers cracks and boulders. Rumbling Bald faces south, which makes it a good winter pick, while Whiteside has walls pointing every direction so you can chase sun or shade. Ice depends on the cold and is unreliable. The rock varies from crag to crag.

wa_northwest.blurb: The far northwest corner of Washington stretches from the Puget Sound coast and islands inland through the Skagit valley to the North Cascades. The mix is wide: sport is most common, followed by trad, alpine objectives, bouldering and a scattering of mountaineering, scrambles, ice and mixed. Rock climbs concentrate between 5.8 and 5.11, with a hard tail beyond. Highway 20 brings alpine granite spires, mostly multipitch trad, best in summer once snow retreats. The San Juan, Fidalgo and Whidbey islands lean toward sport, trad and boulders near the water, and Bellingham and the Mt Baker Highway add bouldering and bolted climbing. Darrington and the Mountain Loop Highway are known for slabby granite domes and long moderate multipitch lines. Rock type changes sharply from one area to the next, so check each crag.

ut_indian_creek.blurb: Indian Creek is a remote desert canyon in southeast Utah, in the northern part of Bears Ears National Monument, with Monticello as the closest town. Red Wingate sandstone cliffs are split by long, parallel cracks of every size, from thin finger seams to offwidths. Climbing is almost entirely trad, mostly single-pitch, with just a handful of sport and boulder problems. Grades pile up at 5.10 to 5.12, with a good number of 5.9 and a thin tail of harder lines, and few easy options for novices. Crack technique matters more than strength, and the rack is often many pieces of the same size. The sandstone is fragile when wet and its grit can scrape skin. Cell service is absent, and a strong top-rope culture lets climbers sample cracks of many widths.

ut_southern_wasatch.blurb: Spread along the southern end of the Wasatch Range, south of Salt Lake City, this group of canyons around Provo and Utah Valley is led by sport climbing, with boulders, trad, ice and mixed routes behind it. Most rock grades land between 5.9 and 5.12, with a good supply of 5.10 and 5.11 and a hard top end. American Fork Canyon is the sport hub, with steep, pocketed limestone and a narrow canyon where trees shade belayers. Rock Canyon is gentler, with a trad, sport and top-rope mix, mostly easier than 5.10; the rock turns from quartzite near the mouth to limestone higher up, and routes on both walls let you pick shade or sun. Provo Canyon is better known for its ice. Smaller canyons such as Santaquin and Hobble Creek add quieter options.
